client: Ever since my grandmother passed away last month, family gatherings have been really hard for me. Everyone else seems to be moving on, but her absence feels so heavy, like there's this huge void that no one else notices. I’m not sure if talking about it will change anything—it’s not like it’ll bring her back.
therapist:
I hear how deeply you're feeling your grandmother's absence, especially when others seem to be moving forward while you're carrying this weight. It makes sense that family gatherings feel different now—we often notice these empty spaces most acutely during traditions and togetherness. 

What thoughts come up for you when you notice that difference between your experience and others'?

client: I just keep thinking "why aren't they as sad as I am?" It makes me angry sometimes, like maybe they didn't love her as much. But then I feel guilty for judging them. Mostly I just sit there feeling like I'm the only one still stuck in this grief.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying some really complex feelings—anger, guilt, and deep sadness—all swirling together in this grief. That sense of being "stuck" while others move on can feel so isolating. 

I'm curious—have you noticed if the anger and guilt tend to follow any particular pattern when you're at these gatherings?

client: It usually happens when someone brings up a happy memory of her and everyone laughs. I get this tight feeling in my chest like "how can they laugh when she's gone?" But then I remember she would have wanted us to laugh, and that just makes me feel worse for being angry. It's all so confusing.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught in a painful cycle where happy memories trigger anger, then guilt, and then confusion—that tightness in your chest is your grief speaking loudly. And while you know intellectually what your grandmother would have wanted, that knowledge doesn't automatically ease the raw feelings, does it? 

What happens if you allow yourself to sit with just one of those feelings at a time—say, the sadness—without judging it or comparing it to others' reactions?

client: I've tried that, but the sadness just overwhelms me. It feels like if I really let myself feel it, I'll completely fall apart in front of everyone. And that makes me feel weak—like I should be handling this better by now. But trying to push it away isn't working either.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between two painful places—the fear of being overwhelmed by grief if you let it in, and the exhaustion of trying to keep it contained. That "should" about handling it better adds another layer of weight to what's already so heavy. 

What would it feel like to gently challenge that thought—that grieving deeply means you're weak or not handling it well?

client: I guess I've never thought about it that way. When I see others being strong for their families, I admire them—I want to be that person too. But honestly, pretending to be okay is exhausting. Maybe there's no right way to grieve? But that thought scares me—how do I know if I'm not making things worse for myself?
therapist:
It sounds like you're starting to question some of those beliefs about how grief "should" look, even though that uncertainty feels a bit unsettling. That exhaustion you describe from trying to maintain a certain image—that's your system telling you something important. 

What would it feel like to extend the same compassion you have for others' grieving processes to your own experience right now?

client: It's hard to imagine being compassionate with myself right now—it feels like I'm failing at grieving "properly." But I guess I wouldn't judge anyone else this harshly. Maybe I'm just scared that if I let myself feel all this, I'll never stop crying. That thought terrifies me—what if I can't pull myself together again?
therapist:
It sounds like there's a lot of fear wrapped up in your grief—fear of losing control, fear of getting "stuck" in it, and fear of not grieving "right." That self-judgment feels so heavy, doesn't it? Yet you're already noticing something important—that you wouldn't hold others to these same rigid standards. 

What would it feel like to take just one small step toward treating yourself with that same gentleness you'd offer a friend in your position?

client: I guess I could try to let myself cry more when I'm alone, instead of always holding it in. But it still feels scary—like once I start, I might not be able to stop. And part of me worries that if I let myself feel all this, I'll just sink deeper into sadness and never come back up. Is that irrational?
therapist:
It makes complete sense that this feels scary—grief can make the sadness feel bottomless when we first let ourselves fully feel it. But I notice you're already showing such courage in considering this step, even with all these understandable fears.  

That worry about sinking deeper—could we explore what "coming back up" might look like for you? What small signs might show you that the sadness isn't endless after all?

client: Maybe "coming back up" would look like being able to look at her photos without immediately tearing up. But even that feels impossible right now—I still avoid her favorite chair in the living room because it hurts too much. I'm afraid that if I start allowing these feelings, I'll never reach that point of being able to remember her without pain.
therapist:
It sounds like you're holding onto a lot of fear about what might happen if you truly allow yourself to feel this grief—like it might keep you from ever reaching a place where memories feel more bittersweet than painful. That avoidance of her chair and photos shows how much you're trying to protect yourself from that hurt. 

Could we explore what it might look like to take one small, gentle step toward those memories—maybe spending just a moment near her chair or looking at one photo—while reminding yourself that you can pause or step away whenever you need to?

client: I could try sitting near her chair for just a minute, but my hands are shaking just thinking about it. What if all the sadness comes rushing out and I can't handle it? Part of me thinks I should wait until I feel stronger, but I've been telling myself that for weeks and it's not getting any easier.
therapist:
It sounds like you're feeling both the pull to try this gentle step and the very real fear of being overwhelmed—those shaking hands show just how much courage this would take. While the "wait until you're stronger" thought makes sense, I notice you're also recognizing that avoidance hasn't made it easier either. 

What would feel like enough support to try this—whether that's planning who to call afterward, setting a timer, or having some comfort nearby?

client: Maybe I could keep my phone nearby to text my sister afterward—she's been pretty understanding about all this. But I'm still scared that once I let myself feel this, I'll somehow lose the memory of how she was when she was alive and only remember the sadness. That probably doesn't make sense, but that's how it feels.
therapist:
It sounds like there's a deep fear that fully feeling your grief might somehow overshadow the beautiful memories of your grandmother—that's such a tender and understandable worry. Having your sister available afterward sounds like a thoughtful way to ground yourself in support if things feel overwhelming.  

What do you think about starting with something small, like just sitting near her chair while holding onto one specific happy memory of her—could that help keep that positive connection present while you take this step?
